sections.html:
• Name: Gold-ringed cowry
  • Other names: Cowrie snail, Ring cowrie, Ring top cowrie
  • Scientific name: Monetaria annulus (previously Cypraea annulus)
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Type: Saltwater snail
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Water type: SG 1.021–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore/detritivore
  • Temperament: Peaceful
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour form: Purplish blue or white

Monetaria annulus is one of the most common species in the Cypraeidae family. These snails are widely distributed in the Indo-West Pacific from tropical to temperate areas.

The northern limit is observed in Boso, Japan, and the southern limit is in Algoa Bay, South Africa.

Gold-ringed cowries are usually found in the middle and lower intertidal areas in shallow water, tide pools, under stones, or among seagrasses. They inhabit rocky, muddy, and sandy shores at depths of 6.5 ft (2 metres).

Because of their small size, there are no minimum requirements. Even nano marine tanks (10 gallons or 40 litres) will be good enough for a few Gold-ringed cowry snails.

Beginners should understand that small tanks have potential problems:

  • It can be difficult to keep water parameters stable.
  • It can be hard for the snails to find enough food, and feeding problems can occur.

Gold-ringed cowry snails are low-maintenance and easy to care for. They do not require large tanks and are fairly forgiving when it comes to water conditions.

Gold-ringed cowries are completely reef safe. Their small size will not allow them to bulldoze through corals, so they will not damage anything in a reef tank, and there is no need to worry about them snacking on corals. Just do not starve them.

Temperature: they prefer warm water of 80–86°F (27–30°C), but can easily tolerate temperatures down to 72°F (22°C). Temperature directly affects calcification: according to a study, calcification accelerated as temperature increased between 70°F (21°C) and 91°F (33°C), and slowed drastically at 93°F (34°C).

pH: maintain 8.1–8.5. The same research noted snails found in waters with a pH of 7.03–7.68.

Hardness: keep 8–12 dKH.

SG: 1.021–1.025.

Calcium and magnesium: calcium of 400–450 ppm and magnesium of 1250–1350 are optimal.

Nitrate: less than 20 ppm.

Lighting: since they are nocturnal, they do not need much light. In nature they live in areas protected from sunlight such as coral reefs, rock pools and seagrass leaves. If you keep corals and fish in the tank, lighting should suit their needs.

Filtration: no special requirements. A filter suited to the tank size is enough.

Substrate: smooth gravel and rocks are best because they are better for algae growth.

Decorations: decor replicates the natural habitat and provides hiding places for the snails. It also provides surface area for algae and diatom growth, so any decor is a good choice for a marine tank with Gold-ringed cowries.

These snails are primarily herbivorous. In the wild, they mostly eat algae, detritus, diatoms, cyanobacteria, and slime that builds up on rocks. They are great scavengers.

In aquariums, they act as a clean-up crew against algae and detritus. Depending on the tank setup, once they have eaten all (or most) of the algae, they may need supplemental feeding for long-term maintenance.

If there is no algae in the tank, give them algae tablets or at least any type of fish, shrimp or crab food.

Gold-ringed cowries are non-aggressive and docile by nature, focused only on grazing and exploring. They are primarily active during the night and often spend the daytime hiding and resting.

They usually do not burrow; instead they climb on surfaces and explore their surroundings.

Although they are found in high densities in the wild, they are not social. They do not care much about other snails unless they decide to mate, and like most snail species they are solitary.

  • Social: No
  • Active: At night
  • Peaceful: Yes
  • Burrowers: No
The shell length of females (22–26 mm) is larger than that of males (17–24 mm).

Breeding cowries in a home aquarium can be a complex task because of the specific environmental conditions required for successful reproduction. Water quality, temperature and the availability of suitable food are crucial. Currently, the pet industry depends on wild-caught animals.

  • The life cycle of intertidal cowries consists of the veliger, juvenile, callus-building, and adult stages.
  • Monetaria annulus has 2 reproductive seasons, in spring and from late summer to winter.
  • Veliger larvae hatch from eggs laid by females on the substrate.
  • Free-swimming veliger larvae spend their planktonic life in the pelagic zone.
  • The larvae settle to the bottom, undergoing the first metamorphosis.
  • Cowries develop a juvenile shell after settlement.
  • The growth of the juvenile shell continues until the shell aperture narrows, producing teeth.
  • Cowries thicken the callus by coating the outer surface of juvenile shells with calcareous materials in the pre-adult stage.

In 1758, this species was described by Carl Linnaeus as Cypraea annulus. In the early 2000s a revision reclassified it as Monetaria annulus. It may have several subspecies (var. alboguttata, meli, camelorum, noumeensis, sublitorea, obvelata), but discussions are ongoing as some believe certain subspecies could be distinct species.

The genus name "Monetaria" derives from the Latin "Moneta", meaning money or coin, referring to the historical use of cowry shells as currency. The species name "annulus" is Latin for ring or circle, referring to the ring patterns on the shells.

Description: the shell is smooth and slippery with small spots, purplish blue or white. Shell shape varies widely with genetic, geographic, ecological and sexual variation; for example, shells in open waters are usually more globular than those in semi-open areas. The blotch is generally golden yellow and ring-shaped. There is a protrusion of the columella and small labial teeth, and the aperture is fairly narrow. Adults are typically 0.8–1 inch (2–2.5 cm), occasionally 1.2 inches (3 cm). Cowries stop growing after building the callus. They can elongate their mantle to completely cover the shell.

Lifespan: there is no official data for the wild; in aquariums it is generally 3 to 5 years.

Difference from Monetaria moneta:

Monetaria annulusMonetaria moneta
Shapemore ovularrhomboidal
Apertureslightly widernarrower
Labial teethgenerally longer, grooves between them more definedgenerally shorter and finer
Coloration/shell patterndistinctive gold ringno ring
